title: What would happen if a giant asteroid crashed into Earth?
byline: Báo Khoa học và Đời sống
excerpt: A collision from a large celestial body could cause catastrophic damage, affecting the climate and ecosystems.

A collision from a large celestial body could cause catastrophic damage, affecting the climate and ecosystems.

Near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) are celestial bodies whose orbits bring them close to our planet's orbit. Most are harmless, but some, ranging in size from hundreds of meters to kilometers, are capable of causing catastrophe if they collide.

NASA classifies an object as a Potentially Hazardous Asteroid (PHAs) when its estimated diameter is approximately 140 meters or more and its minimum orbital intersection distance with Earth is no more than 7.5 million kilometers. However, this does not mean that the object will definitely collide with our planet.

One of the celestial bodies of particular interest to scientists is Bennu, which has a diameter of approximately 490 meters. Discovered in 1999, this object became the target of NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission. The spacecraft collected samples from Bennu in 2020 and returned them to Earth in 2023. Bennu has a very small probability of collision in the distant future, notably in 2182. According to the European Space Agency's (ESA) risk assessment, the probability of collision is estimated at approximately 1 in 2,700. Nevertheless, scientists continue to monitor its orbit to update their predictions.

The asteroid Bennu was photographed by the OSIRIS-REx spacecraft. Photo: science.nasa.gov

Another notable asteroid is 1950 DA, first discovered in 1950. With an estimated diameter of about 1.3 km, it is significantly larger than Bennu. Orbital calculations once determined a collision probability in 2880, although the probability is very low, about 1 in 51,020 according to ESA data. This is an example of how astronomers must predict asteroid movements over long periods of centuries, even millennia.

Apophis also caused concern among scientists after its discovery in 2004. With a maximum length of approximately 450 meters, this celestial body was initially assessed to have a collision risk in 2029, 2036, and 2068. However, more accurate radar observations have ruled out the risk of collision for at least the next 100 years. On April 13, 2029, Apophis will fly past Earth at a distance of only 32,000 km from the surface, closer than the orbits of many geostationary satellites.

Image of asteroid Apophis. nasa.gov

The most terrifying aspect of a large asteroid impact isn't just its direct destructive power. An object with a diameter of about 140 meters could create an explosion equivalent to millions of tons of TNT, causing widespread destruction. If an object with a diameter of about 1 kilometer were to collide, the dust and debris ejected into the atmosphere could affect the climate, crops, and ecosystems on a global scale. Much larger objects have the potential to cause mass extinctions, similar to the event believed to have contributed to the end of the dinosaur era about 66 million years ago.

A recent notable case is asteroid 2024 YR4. When it was first discovered in late 2024, it had a significant probability of colliding with Earth on December 22, 2032, prompting close monitoring by international astronomical agencies. However, additional observations helped NASA rule out a significant risk to Earth in 2032 and the following century. By March 2026, observations from the James Webb Space Telescope also helped rule out the possibility of this celestial body colliding with the Moon.

Faced with the threat from such celestial objects, scientists are developing various planetary defense options. A notable achievement was NASA's DART mission in 2022, when the spacecraft deliberately crashed into the asteroid Dimorphos to test the possibility of altering the celestial body's orbit through kinetic impact. The experiment was successful, demonstrating that humans can influence the motion of an asteroid if the threat is detected early enough.

Currently, no asteroids have been identified as posing a significant collision threat to Earth in the near future. However, continuously observing the sky, detecting unknown celestial bodies, and accurately calculating their orbits remains a crucial task. In the battle for planetary defense, time is humanity's greatest advantage.
